flashcards.definition: Security and management duties are split between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider always owns the physical datacenter, network and hosts. The customer always owns their data, devices, accounts and identities. Everything in between (OS, apps, network controls) shifts toward the provider as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS.
flashcards.analogy: Renting a car: the rental company maintains the engine and brakes, but you are responsible for how you drive and what you leave on the back seat. With an Azure VM you patch the OS; with Microsoft 365 Microsoft patches everything but you still own who has access to your files.

flashcards.definition: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) rents raw compute, storage and networking; you manage the OS and above. PaaS (Platform as a Service) provides a managed runtime; you manage only your app and data. SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers a finished application; you just configure and use it.
flashcards.analogy: Pizza as a service: IaaS is buying the kitchen time (Azure Virtual Machines), PaaS is a take-and-bake pizza (Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database), SaaS is pizza delivered to your door (Microsoft 365, Outlook).

flashcards.definition: Capital Expenditure (CapEx) is a large up-front spend on physical assets such as servers and datacenters, depreciated over time. Operational Expenditure (OpEx) is ongoing spend on services as you consume them. The cloud's consumption-based model shifts IT spending from CapEx to OpEx.
flashcards.analogy: Buying a house (CapEx) versus paying rent (OpEx). Instead of buying 50 servers for a peak you might never hit, you pay per hour for Azure VMs and stop paying when you shut them down.

flashcards.definition: Designing a service to stay accessible with minimal downtime, even when components fail. It is usually expressed as an uptime percentage in a Service Level Agreement (SLA), for example 99.9% or 99.99%, and achieved through redundancy across hardware, zones or regions.
flashcards.analogy: A plane with two engines: if one fails it can still land. Running two or more VMs across Availability Zones behind a load balancer keeps your app online if one datacenter has an outage.

flashcards.definition: Scalability is the ability to add or remove resources to handle demand: vertically (scale up to a bigger machine) or horizontally (scale out to more machines). Elasticity is scaling that happens automatically and in near real time as demand rises and falls, so you only pay for what you need.
flashcards.analogy: Scalability is a restaurant that can add tables when it gets popular. Elasticity is tables that appear on their own at the lunch rush and vanish at 3 p.m. In Azure, Virtual Machine Scale Sets with autoscale rules add VMs when CPU spikes and remove them when it drops.

flashcards.definition: Public cloud is owned and run by a provider and shared by many customers, with no CapEx to scale. Private cloud is used by a single organization, either on-premises or hosted, offering full control at higher cost. Hybrid cloud combines both, letting data and apps move between them. Multi-cloud uses more than one public provider.
flashcards.analogy: Public is a hotel, private is your own house, hybrid is your house plus a hotel room when relatives visit. Azure Arc lets you manage on-premises and other-cloud servers from Azure as part of a hybrid strategy.

flashcards.definition: An Azure region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters connected by a low-latency network. Many regions are paired with another region in the same geography at least 300 miles away where possible, so that platform updates are rolled out to one at a time and recovery is prioritized during a broad outage.
flashcards.analogy: Like a bank having branches in two cities: if a disaster closes one, the other keeps your records safe. You choose regions to keep data close to users and to meet data residency rules.

flashcards.definition: Physically separate locations within an Azure region, each made up of one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking. Zone-enabled regions have a minimum of three zones. Spreading resources across zones protects against a single datacenter failure.
flashcards.analogy: Three separate buildings on one campus, each with its own generator. If a fire knocks out one building, the other two keep running your zone-redundant VMs and storage.

flashcards.term: Resource Hierarchy: Management Groups, Subscriptions, Resource Groups
flashcards.definition: Resources (VMs, databases) live in exactly one Resource Group, a logical container sharing a lifecycle. Resource groups live in a Subscription, a unit of billing and access boundaries. Subscriptions can be organized under Management Groups so policies and RBAC apply to many subscriptions at once. Settings applied at a higher level are inherited below.
flashcards.analogy: A filing cabinet (management group) holds drawers (subscriptions), each with folders (resource groups), each with documents (resources). Deleting a folder throws away every document in it, so put resources with the same lifecycle in the same resource group.

flashcards.definition: Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS: full control of the OS, ideal for lift-and-shift or custom software. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a managed Kubernetes service for orchestrating containerized microservices; Azure manages the control plane and you manage your container workloads.
flashcards.analogy: A VM is renting a whole apartment and furnishing it yourself. AKS is a managed shipping port that loads, stacks and moves standard containers for you, restarting any that fall off the dock.

flashcards.definition: Azure App Service is a PaaS for hosting web apps, REST APIs and mobile back ends with built-in scaling, deployment slots and patching. Azure Functions is serverless, event-driven compute: code runs in response to a trigger (HTTP request, queue message, timer) and on the Consumption plan you pay only while it executes.
flashcards.analogy: App Service is a shop that is always open. Functions is a vending machine that wakes up only when someone presses a button, such as resizing an image every time it lands in Blob Storage.

flashcards.definition: An Azure Virtual Network (VNet) is your private network in Azure, enabling resources to talk to each other, to the internet and to on-premises networks. Subnets segment it, and VNet peering connects VNets. Azure Load Balancer distributes incoming traffic (Layer 4, TCP/UDP) across healthy VMs to improve availability.
flashcards.analogy: A VNet is a private office floor with locked doors between departments (subnets). The Load Balancer is the receptionist sending each visitor to whichever available colleague is free.

flashcards.definition: A VPN Gateway sends encrypted traffic between Azure and on-premises over the public internet (site-to-site, point-to-site). ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated connection through a connectivity provider that does not traverse the public internet, offering higher reliability, consistent latency and higher bandwidth.
flashcards.analogy: VPN Gateway is an armored van driving on public highways. ExpressRoute is your own private railway track straight into the Azure datacenter.

flashcards.term: Azure Storage Services: Blob, Files, Disks
flashcards.definition: Blob Storage holds massive amounts of unstructured object data (images, video, backups) accessed over HTTP/HTTPS. Azure Files provides fully managed file shares over SMB or NFS that can be mounted by cloud or on-premises machines. Azure Disks are block-level managed disks attached to Azure VMs.
flashcards.analogy: Blob is a giant warehouse of labeled boxes, Files is a shared network drive everyone in the office maps as Z:, and Disks are the hard drives plugged directly into each VM.

flashcards.term: Blob Access Tiers: Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive
flashcards.definition: Hot is for frequently accessed data (highest storage cost, lowest access cost). Cool is for infrequently accessed data stored at least 30 days. Cold is for rarely accessed data stored at least 90 days. Archive is offline storage for data kept at least 180 days; it is the cheapest to store but must be rehydrated, which can take hours, before it can be read.
flashcards.analogy: Hot is your desk, Cool is the filing cabinet, Cold is the basement, and Archive is an off-site vault where you have to request a box and wait for delivery. Compliance logs you must keep for 7 years belong in Archive.

flashcards.definition: A set of tools to analyze, monitor and optimize Azure spending. It provides cost analysis, budgets with alerts, recommendations and exports. Related tools include the Pricing Calculator (estimate the cost of new resources) and the TCO Calculator (compare on-premises costs with Azure).
flashcards.analogy: A household budgeting app linked to your bank: it shows where the money went and pings you when you're at 80% of your monthly grocery budget. Set an Azure budget alert so the team hears about runaway spend before the invoice arrives.

flashcards.definition: A service for creating, assigning and managing rules that enforce standards on resources, for example allowed regions, required tags or allowed VM sizes. Policies can deny non-compliant deployments, audit existing ones, or remediate them. Groups of policies are called initiatives. Policy governs what resources look like, not who can act.
flashcards.analogy: Building codes for your cloud city: no matter who the builder is, you cannot put up a house without fire exits. A policy can block anyone from deploying resources outside West Europe.

flashcards.definition: Azure RBAC controls who can do what on which resources. A role assignment combines a security principal (user, group, service principal or managed identity), a role definition (such as Owner, Contributor or Reader) and a scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource). Permissions are inherited down the hierarchy. Grant the least privilege needed.
flashcards.analogy: Hotel key cards: housekeeping cards open guest rooms on one floor, the manager's card opens every room, and a guest's card opens only their own room. Give a developer Contributor on their team's resource group, not Owner on the whole subscription.

flashcards.definition: Locks prevent accidental changes to resources, resource groups or subscriptions, and they apply to everyone, even Owners. CanNotDelete (shown as Delete) lets users read and modify but not delete. ReadOnly lets users read but not modify or delete. Locks are inherited, and a lock must be removed before the protected action can happen.
flashcards.analogy: A child-proof lock on the medicine cabinet: it doesn't matter who you are, you have to deliberately unlock it first. Put a Delete lock on the production database's resource group.

flashcards.definition: A free, personalized recommendation engine that analyzes your resource configuration and usage and suggests improvements in five categories: Reliability, Security, Performance, Cost and Operational Excellence.
flashcards.analogy: A financial advisor reviewing your accounts and saying: cancel that unused gym membership. Advisor might tell you a VM has averaged 3% CPU for two weeks and should be resized or shut down.

flashcards.definition: A comprehensive platform for collecting, analyzing and acting on metrics and logs from Azure, on-premises and other clouds. It includes Log Analytics for querying logs, Application Insights for application performance monitoring, and alerts with action groups. Azure Service Health, by contrast, reports on the health of Azure services themselves.
flashcards.analogy: The dashboard and warning lights in your car: speed, fuel, engine temperature, and a beep when something crosses a threshold. Set an alert to email on-call when web app response time exceeds 2 seconds.

flashcards.definition: Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service (formerly Azure Active Directory). It provides authentication, single sign-on (SSO), multifactor authentication (MFA), Conditional Access and identity protection for Microsoft 365, Azure and thousands of SaaS apps. Entra Connect syncs on-premises AD identities to the cloud.
flashcards.analogy: A passport office for your organization: one trusted ID gets you through every border (app) you are allowed into, and suspicious travelers get extra checks (MFA) at the gate.

flashcards.definition: A security model that assumes breach and treats every request as if it came from an uncontrolled network. Its three principles are: verify explicitly (authenticate and authorize using all available signals), use least privilege access (just-in-time and just-enough access), and assume breach (segment access and minimize blast radius).
flashcards.analogy: An airport where you show your boarding pass at every gate, not just at the entrance. Conditional Access in Entra ID requires MFA when someone signs in from an unknown device, even if their password is correct.

flashcards.definition: A layered security strategy so that if one layer is breached the next one still protects data. The layers are: physical security, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, and data at the center.
flashcards.analogy: A medieval castle: moat, outer wall, inner wall, guards, and a locked vault holding the crown jewels. In Azure: datacenter security, Entra ID with MFA, Azure DDoS Protection and Firewall, network security groups, patched VMs, secure code, and encrypted data.

questions.question: Your company is migrating an on-premises application to Azure Virtual Machines. Under the shared responsibility model, which task remains the customer's responsibility?
options: Maintaining the physical datacenter's power and cooling
Applying security patches to the guest operating system
Securing the physical hosts that run the hypervisor
questions.explanation: Azure VMs are IaaS. In IaaS, Microsoft is responsible for the physical datacenter, network and hosts, while the customer manages the guest OS, including patching, plus applications, data and identities.

questions.question: A startup wants to deploy a web app without managing servers, operating systems or runtime patching, but it still wants to write and deploy its own code. Which cloud service model fits best?
questions.explanation: PaaS (for example Azure App Service) provides a managed platform: the provider handles the OS, runtime and patching, and the customer deploys and manages only their application code and data. IaaS would require managing the OS; SaaS would not allow custom code.

questions.question: Your finance team wants to stop making large up-front purchases of servers and instead pay only for the IT resources it consumes each month. Which expenditure model is this?
questions.explanation: Paying for services as you consume them is operational expenditure (OpEx). CapEx is up-front spending on physical infrastructure that is depreciated over time. Cloud computing's consumption-based model is an OpEx model.

questions.question: An online retailer's traffic triples every evening and drops overnight. They want resources to be added and removed automatically to match demand. Which cloud benefit describes this?
questions.explanation: Elasticity is the ability to automatically and dynamically add or remove resources in response to changing demand, so you pay only for what you need. Fault tolerance and disaster recovery are about surviving failures, not tracking demand.

questions.question: A hospital must keep patient records in its own datacenter for regulatory reasons, but wants to use Azure to burst its analytics workloads during peak periods. Which cloud model should it use?
questions.explanation: A hybrid cloud combines on-premises (private) infrastructure with public cloud services, letting sensitive data stay on-premises while workloads burst into Azure. Public-only would move the records; private-only would not use Azure capacity.

questions.question: Microsoft guarantees 99.95% uptime for a service in its Service Level Agreement. Which cloud concept does this SLA primarily describe?
questions.explanation: An SLA uptime percentage is a measure of high availability: how much of the time the service is guaranteed to be accessible. Higher percentages mean less permitted downtime (99.95% allows roughly 22 minutes per month).

questions.question: Your database server is running out of memory, so you resize the VM from 8 GB to 32 GB of RAM. What type of scaling is this?
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling (scaling up) adds more capacity such as CPU or RAM to an existing resource. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more instances of a resource, such as more VMs.

questions.question: You need to ensure that your application stays available if a single Azure datacenter fails, while keeping all resources in the same region. What should you use?
questions.explanation: Availability Zones are physically separate datacenter locations within one region, each with independent power, cooling and networking. Deploying across zones protects against a datacenter failure without leaving the region. Region pairs span two different regions.

questions.question: A developer deletes a resource group that contains three VMs, a storage account and a virtual network. What happens to those resources?
options: They are moved to the default resource group
They remain running but become unmanaged
They are all deleted along with the resource group
Only the virtual network is deleted
questions.explanation: A resource group is a lifecycle container: deleting it deletes every resource inside it. That is why resources that share a lifecycle are grouped together, and why resource locks are useful on important resource groups.

questions.question: You want to run a small piece of code every time a new image is uploaded to Blob Storage, and you only want to pay while the code is running. Which Azure service is the best fit?
options: Azure App Service on a dedicated plan
questions.explanation: Azure Functions is serverless, event-driven compute. A Blob Storage trigger can run the function on every upload, and on the Consumption plan you are billed only for execution time. VMs, AKS and dedicated App Service plans incur cost while idle.

questions.question: Your company requires a private, dedicated connection between its on-premises datacenter and Azure that does not travel over the public internet. What should you use?
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private connection through a connectivity provider that does not traverse the public internet, with higher reliability and consistent latency. VPN Gateway connections are encrypted but still go over the public internet. VNet peering connects Azure VNets to each other, not to on-premises.

questions.question: You must retain audit logs for seven years for compliance. They will almost never be read, and a retrieval delay of several hours is acceptable. Which Blob access tier minimizes storage cost?
questions.explanation: The Archive tier has the lowest storage cost and is designed for data kept at least 180 days that is rarely accessed. Data is stored offline and must be rehydrated (which can take hours) before reading, which is acceptable here.

questions.question: Several on-premises servers and Azure VMs need to mount the same shared folder using the SMB protocol. Which Azure Storage service should you use?
questions.explanation: Azure Files offers fully managed file shares accessible via SMB (and NFS) that can be mounted concurrently by cloud and on-premises machines. Blob Storage is object storage over HTTP, Disks attach to a single VM as block storage, and Queue Storage is for messages.

questions.question: Your team wants to deploy a microservices application packaged as containers and needs automated orchestration, scaling and self-healing of those containers. Which service should you choose?
questions.explanation: AKS is a managed Kubernetes service for orchestrating containers: it handles scheduling, scaling and restarting unhealthy containers, while Azure manages the Kubernetes control plane.

questions.question: Your organization must ensure that resources can only be deployed to the East US and West Europe regions across all subscriptions. What should you use?
questions.explanation: Azure Policy enforces rules about resource properties, such as allowed locations, and can deny non-compliant deployments. Assigning it at a management group applies it to all subscriptions below. RBAC controls who can act, not what resources look like.

questions.question: A contractor needs to manage VMs in one resource group but must not be able to grant access to other users. Following least privilege, which built-in role should you assign, and at which scope?
options: User Access Administrator at the subscription
questions.explanation: Contributor can create and manage resources but cannot assign roles. Scoping it to the single resource group follows least privilege. Owner can also grant access, Reader cannot make changes, and User Access Administrator manages access rather than resources.

questions.question: You want to prevent anyone, including subscription Owners, from accidentally deleting a production database, while still allowing its configuration to be changed. What should you apply?
options: An Azure Policy with the Audit effect
questions.explanation: A CanNotDelete lock allows reading and modifying a resource but blocks deletion for all users, including Owners, until the lock is removed. A ReadOnly lock would also block configuration changes.

questions.question: Which Azure service provides free, personalized recommendations across reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence, such as resizing underused VMs?
questions.explanation: Azure Advisor analyzes your configuration and usage telemetry and gives best-practice recommendations in those five categories. Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs, and Service Health reports on the health of Azure services.

questions.question: Your company wants users to sign in once to access Microsoft 365, Azure and third-party SaaS apps, with MFA required for risky sign-ins. Which service provides this?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is the cloud identity service providing single sign-on, multifactor authentication and Conditional Access for Microsoft and third-party apps.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Zero Trust security model?
options: Trust all devices inside the corporate network perimeter
Verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach
Rely on a strong firewall as the single line of defense
Grant administrators permanent access to all resources
questions.explanation: Zero Trust assumes breach and verifies every request as though it came from an open network. Its guiding principles are verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach. Trusting the network perimeter is the traditional model Zero Trust replaces.

questions.question: In the defense-in-depth model, which layer is at the center and is ultimately being protected by all the other layers?
questions.explanation: Defense in depth wraps data, at the center, in layers: physical security, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, and finally data. If an attacker breaches one layer, the next layer still protects the data.

questions.question: Your manager wants an email notification when the monthly Azure spending for a subscription reaches 80% of a set amount. What should you configure?
options: A budget in Microsoft Cost Management
questions.explanation: Budgets in Microsoft Cost Management let you set a spending threshold and send alerts when actual or forecasted cost reaches percentages of it. The Pricing and TCO calculators estimate costs before deployment; they don't monitor spending.
